01 The Opportunity

Picture standing at the edge of 160 acres in North Park, a snow-capped range filling the horizon and public land running along your boundary. That is the picture this property paints, and it is yours to fill in.

About ten miles east of Walden, the parcel sits in the wide, open valley of Jackson County. The listing describes a boundary with BLM and State Trust Land, a partially fenced perimeter, minimal flood risk, and zoning the MLS marks as appropriate for four or more horses. Electric lines are reported to run through the property.

What it does not have is just as important to you. There is no well, no sewer, no HOA and no metro district. That means the build is yours to plan, the water is yours to solve, and the costs of that plan are yours to price before you commit. This report walks through both sides.

This report describes the property from the data supplied and offers an opinion on it. It is not a valuation or a comparative market analysis.

05 Water, Power & Access

What is there, and what you would be adding.

Raw land is priced against everything it does not yet have. Here is what the MLS says about each essential, and what to confirm.

Water

You would need a well.

MLS: Need well · no water meter · no irrigation water rights · no ditches

Nothing is drilled today and no water rights are listed, so this is dryland ground. In Colorado, a household well is permitted through the State Engineer's office. For parcels of 35 acres or more, a domestic and livestock permit is generally available: one well per parcel, limited yield, and limited outdoor irrigation.

Whether this parcel qualifies, and whether the undivided-interest question affects who can apply, is for the Division of Water Resources to answer. You may want to talk to a local well driller about depth and yield in this part of North Park before you count on a figure.

Power

Electric is reported on the property.

MLS field says "No utilities" · listing remarks say electricity runs through

These two statements do not conflict if a line crosses the land without a service point on it. A line crossing the property is not the same as service being available to your building site.

Ask the serving electric utility where the nearest service point is, what an extension to your chosen site would involve, and whether any easements are recorded.

Sewer

An on-site septic system.

MLS: No water / sewer · well needed

With no municipal sewer, a home would need a permitted on-site wastewater system. Soils, groundwater depth and frost depth at your chosen site drive what the county will approve.

Soil and percolation testing belongs early in your planning, ahead of a house design.

Access

A county road the county does not maintain.

MLS: County road / not county maintained · partially fenced

This wording usually means the county owns the right-of-way but does not plow, grade or repair it. In North Park, where annual snowfall is heavy, that decides how and when you can get to your land.

Confirm recorded legal access to the parcel, who maintains the road in winter, and what you would need to do for a driveway.

Zoning and building eligibility. The MLS shows zoning as "Res," possible usage as "Farm/Ranch," and "Number of living units allowed" as "Not applicable." Those fields do not tell you whether, where and how many dwellings Jackson County will permit on this land. Confirm that directly with the county before you plan around a house, a second dwelling, or guest quarters.
06 Public Land & Recreation

Next to public land is not the same as on it.

The listing highlights a boundary with BLM and State Trust Land and "direct access to prime hunting and outdoor recreation." Here is what that does and does not mean.

BLM land

Generally open to the public.

Bureau of Land Management land is generally open for public recreation, subject to its rules and any local closures. Whether you can step onto it directly from this parcel depends on where the shared boundary falls and on the legal access to your own land. Walk the boundary on a survey and the BLM map together.

State Trust Land

Usually closed unless leased for recreation.

The Colorado State Land Board states that the general public may use trust land only when it is leased for public recreation, and that a listing describing a property as bordering state land can mislead buyers about access. Bordering trust land does not give you the right to enter or use it. Ask whether this adjoining parcel is in a public-access program or under a recreation lease.

  • MLS saysBorders BLM and State Trust Land
  • Listing remarksDirect access to prime hunting and outdoor recreation
  • Photos showMule deer, high-country sage and grass
  • LicensingColorado Parks and Wildlife
Hunting. Hunting here is governed by Colorado Parks and Wildlife licensing, season dates and game management units, none of which come with the land. Check the unit that covers this parcel, the license and draw rules for the species you care about, and any state or federal rules where you plan to hunt, including on neighboring public parcels.
The strongest recreation value you can count on is the 160 acres you would own. Treat any use of the neighboring public parcels as a bonus you confirm, not a guarantee.
07 The Balanced View

Highlights & considerations.

An honest ledger: what makes this land special, and what deserves a harder look before you fall for it.

+ Highlights

  • Real acreage. 160 acres is a full quarter section of high-country ground, with room for a home site, pasture, trails and privacy.
  • The view. The listing and the photo set both show a snow-capped range across open ground.
  • Public land on the boundary. BLM and State Trust Land border the parcel, which protects the feeling of space around you.
  • Electric nearby. Lines are reported on the property, which can shorten the path to service.
  • Low carrying cost. Taxes were $3,466 for 2024, with no HOA and no metro district.
  • Flexible use. The MLS lists farm and ranch as a possible use and horse-appropriate zoning.
  • Minimal flood risk. The MLS shows minimal flood-plain risk.

– Considerations

  • The legal description. It references an undivided interest and one-third interests from two accounts. Get title clarity first.
  • No well and no sewer. Water and wastewater are your costs and your timeline, and both depend on permits and site conditions.
  • "No utilities" versus "electric on property." The MLS says both. Confirm what service is actually available.
  • Access in winter. A county road that is not county maintained, in a valley with heavy snowfall.
  • Public-land access is not automatic. Bordering BLM and State Trust Land is not a right to use either one.
  • Building eligibility is unstated. Zoning "Res" and "living units: not applicable" leave real questions about dwellings.
  • 230 days on the market. Worth asking why, and whether any earlier contract fell apart.

09 Due Diligence

What to confirm, in the order that matters.

Before you make an offer During your due-diligence period Before you build
1
Before an offer

Clarify the legal description and ownership

Ask for a title commitment. Confirm what interest the seller holds in the full 160 acres, what the one-third references mean, and whether any co-owner must sign.

2
Before an offer

Confirm legal access

Verify recorded access from County Road 23C to the parcel, who maintains the road, and what winter access looks like in practice.

3
Before an offer

Define what the public-land borders mean

Locate the BLM boundary on a map. Ask the State Land Board whether the adjoining trust parcel is leased or enrolled for public recreation. Do not assume access.

4
Before an offer

Confirm zoning and building eligibility

Ask Jackson County what the zoning permits here: dwellings, number of dwellings, setbacks, and any limits on occupancy or short-term use.

5
During due diligence

Test the water path

Ask the Division of Water Resources about permit eligibility for this parcel. Talk to a local driller about depth and yield nearby. Confirm what the MLS meant by no water rights.

6
During due diligence

Pin down electric service

Ask the serving utility where service is available, the cost and process to extend it to your site, and any recorded easements across the land.

7
During due diligence

Order a boundary survey

Establish the corners, compare them to the fences, locate any drainage or wetland, and place the log structure on the map.

8
During due diligence

Line up financing early

Raw land is underwritten differently from a home. Review the lender directory and ask each lender about its land-loan terms before you write an offer.

9
Before you build

Soils, septic and the building site

Choose a site, then test it. Septic design, foundation conditions and drainage all follow from where the house sits.

10
Before you build

Plan for the high-country winter

Wind, snow load, propane, internet and cell coverage, and a road that may not be plowed for you all shape what living here is like. Visit in winter if you can.

10 My Take

Here is my honest read, Crystal.

What I like. A full 160 acres with a mountain view and public land on the boundary is hard to come by, and the carrying cost of $3,466 a year with no HOA is light. The setting is the real product here: space, quiet, and a landscape that changes with the season.

What would slow me down. The legal description is the first thing I would resolve, because everything else depends on what is actually being conveyed. After that, legal access in winter, the path to a permitted well, and where electric service really stands. Each of these is solvable. I would want written answers to all of them before spending real money.

What 230 days tells you. The land has been on the market a long time. That is not a flaw on its own, but it is a good reason to ask the listing side about showing activity and whether any earlier contract fell through.

Who this suits. Someone who wants room, silence and the outdoors, who is comfortable with a build-it-yourself timeline, and who is ready for the logistics of a high-country winter. If you want a turnkey place, this is not it. If you want a canvas, it very well may be.

This is my opinion based on the data supplied, not a valuation, appraisal or legal, tax or financial advice.

11 Area Guide

Walden and North Park.

The parcel sits in North Park, a large open valley ringed by mountains. Here is the context you would be living in.

The town

Walden

Walden is the county seat of Jackson County and its only incorporated town, sitting at about 8,100 feet in the middle of North Park. It had roughly 600 residents at the 2020 census. Your land is about ten miles from it, per the listing.

The climate

High, dry and snowy

Walden's climate is semi-arid and close to subalpine, with about 12 inches of precipitation and about 67 inches of snow in an average year. Record lows have gone well below zero. Plan your access, heat, and building details around that.

The wildlife

Elk, moose and waterfowl

Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge, south of Walden, protects nearly 25,000 acres of wetland meadow and upland. Elk winter in the valley, and moose are now seen in the willows along the rivers. The refuge also has a self-guided auto tour off Highway 14.

  • School districtNorth Park R-1 · Walden Elementary · North Park High School
  • State Forest State ParkAbout 23 miles east of Walden on Highway 14
  • Highway 14Crosses Cameron Pass toward Poudre Canyon and Fort Collins. A mountain pass, so check conditions in winter.
  • RecreationHunting, fishing, wildlife viewing, trails, snow sports

Sources: Walden, Colorado (Wikipedia) · Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge (Wikipedia) · Colorado Parks and Wildlife, State Forest State Park directions · Colorado State Land Board, public access on trust land · CSU Extension, Colorado well permits

Legal Description, Title & Ownership Advisory

The legal description in the MLS references an undivided interest and fractional interests traced to other account numbers. Access, Roads & Public Land Advisory

The MLS describes road access as a county road that is not county maintained. Legal and physical access, road maintenance responsibility, winter access, driveway and culvert requirements, and any easements must be independently verified. Adjacency to Bureau of Land Management or Colorado State Land Board trust land does not by itself create a right of public or private access to, across, or onto that land. Colorado State Trust Land is generally closed to the public unless leased or permitted for recreation. Boundaries between private and public land must be confirmed by survey and public land records.

Water, Well, Septic & Utilities Advisory

The MLS indicates that no water or sewer service is present and that a well is needed. Well permit eligibility, depth, yield, water quality, and legal availability of groundwater are determined by the Colorado Division of Water Resources and site conditions, and are not guaranteed. On-site wastewater systems require soil evaluation and local permitting. The MLS reports both "no utilities" and electricity running through the property; availability, location, capacity, and cost of electric, propane, telephone, and internet service must be confirmed with the serving providers. These items represent significant ownership costs and must be thoroughly evaluated prior to purchase.

Water Rights & Mineral Interests

The MLS indicates no irrigation water rights and no irrigation ditches. Water rights, mineral interests, oil, gas, and other subsurface rights are not described in the MLS record and may be reserved, severed, or owned by others. These must be confirmed through title review and public records prior to purchase.

Zoning, Land Use & Building Eligibility

Zoning shown in the MLS ("Res") and the stated possible usage ("Farm/Ranch") are marketing representations and may not reflect the controlling county zoning designation. Whether, where, and how many dwellings or accessory structures may be built, applicable setbacks, building permits, occupancy limits, short-term rental rules, and horse or livestock allowances must be confirmed with Jackson County and any other agency of jurisdiction. Neither Zachary Springborn nor JPAR® Modern Real Estate makes any representation regarding buildability or the legality of any specific use.

Wildfire & Natural Hazard Disclosure

Rural and mountain-valley properties in Northern Colorado may be subject to wildfire, high wind, heavy snow load, drifting, extreme cold, and other natural hazards.
